name: Carla Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drill blast holes at the Kestrel Hill gold mine, an open pit. I take the rig out to the bench, line it up on the pegs the surveyors leave, and drill a pattern of holes, maybe forty or fifty a shift, so the blast crew can load them. It's slow, careful work, you listen to the bit and you feel when the ground changes. I like that it's the same every day, I'll be honest. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the paperwork they keep adding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Walter was a fitter until his back went four years ago, so now he's on a small disability payment and does the garden. Our daughter Ines lives ten minutes away with her two little ones, and our son works on ships and we see him at Christmas if we're lucky. Between Walter's physio and the car breaking down twice, we've got maybe two weeks of money put by. I'm on the lower end of the drill rates. I want to get to sixty-three and then stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, they said the same about the internet and I still drill holes. I'm not one for big opinions. I'd say it at break time and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief, plain and simple. I don't use any of that AI stuff and I don't want to start at fifty-eight. If nothing changes, I get my five years and go home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep turning up, keep my tickets current, and keep trying to put twenty a week in the jar for Walter's physio. Maybe go back to doing the overtime on Saturdays if they offer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like being told the road works are finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the paperwork they keep adding. Is any of that computer-based?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's all on a tablet now, the pre-start checks, the hole depths. I do it, but Ines had to show me twice. I can feel a hard band of rock through my boots, but I can't find the save button on that tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've had a self-drilling rig at another site for a while. Someone sits in an office and it drills the pattern by itself. I don't think Kestrel Hill can afford it yet, but you never know.

S0.say: I'd say they said the same about the internet and I'm still drilling holes. I'm not one for big opinions, so I'd say it once at break and leave it.
S0.think: Privately it would be a plain relief, because I don't use AI and don't want to start now. If nothing changes, I get my five years and go home.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and keeps her tickets current. Tries to put twenty a week aside for her husband's physio and takes Saturday overtime if it's offered.
S0.feel: Calm, like hearing the road works are finished.
S0.quote: I can feel a hard band of rock through my boots, but I can't find the save button on that tablet.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is careful and modest, and her whole plan is to reach sixty-three doing the same job. She is pragmatic rather than political and avoids big statements. The self-drilling rig at another site is already in the back of her mind, even in the mildest picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is change, you can't stop it, but they should do it fairly. Give the older ones a choice and some time. I'm not going to march about it, but I'd say that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the self-drilling rigs come to Kestrel Hill, probably in the next few years. Drilling is perfect for a machine, the pattern's all set by the surveyors. I'd be one of the first off, and I don't have the computer skills to sit in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what they actually announce before I panicked, but I'd cut back right away, no more takeaway, cheaper phone plan, Walter's pickup goes. I'd ask about other jobs on site, maybe the store or the gatehouse. And I'd talk to Ines about whether we could lean on her a bit if it came to it, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a sore tooth I keep touching with my tongue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate to lean on Ines. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got her own two to feed and her husband's on shift work at the abattoir. Parents are supposed to help kids, not the other way round. I've been giving Ines money since she was sixteen, I don't know how to be the one holding out my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning to run the self-drilling rig from the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd try. But I'd be slow, and the young ones would be quicker, and the bosses know that. I don't like my chances against a twenty-five-year-old with a game controller.

S1.say: I'd say change is change and you can't stop it, but it should be done fairly, with a choice and time for the older workers. I wouldn't march, but I'd say that much.
S1.think: Privately, it means self-drilling rigs come to Kestrel Hill and I'd be one of the first off. Drilling is perfect for a machine and I don't have the computer skills to move into the office.
S1.do: Waits for the company's announcement before acting on the job itself, but cuts spending straight away: takeaway, phone plan and her husband's pickup. Asks about store or gatehouse jobs on site and raises with her daughter the idea of leaning on her if needed.
S1.feel: Anxious, like a sore tooth she keeps touching.
S1.quote: I've been giving Ines money since she was sixteen, I don't know how to be the one holding out my hand.
S1.fieldNote: Carla's worry is precise: drilling to a pre-set pattern is easy to automate, and she doubts she could compete for the remote job. Her centre politics show in asking for fairness rather than resistance. The hardest part for her is the thought of taking help from her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say, honestly. If it's everyone, every job, then it's up to the government to sort something out, because there's no other job to go to. That's not me being political, that's just arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be finished. Two years, I'm sixty, no job, Walter on a disability payment, two weeks in the bank. There's no other pit in this valley, there's no other job I know how to do, and there's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd go to the welfare office the day the letter came, and I'd ring the pension fund. We'd probably have to sell the house and move in with Ines, or somewhere cheaper. That's about as far as I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like the rig's sliding off the bench and the brakes don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, is there anything you'd start doing tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save every cent, I suppose, but there's not many cents. Maybe Walter could do a bit of gardening for people, but his back. Two years just means two years of watching it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter. Then I'd go round to Ines and not tell her, just sit in her kitchen and hold the baby. I'd tell her later, once I knew what we were doing.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know what to say, except that if every job goes then the government has to sort something out. That's not politics, it's just arithmetic.
S2.think: Privately, I'd be finished: sixty, no job, a husband on a disability payment and two weeks of savings. There's no other pit in the valley, no other job I know and no time.
S2.do: Goes to the welfare office and rings the pension fund the day the letter arrives. Considers selling the house and moving in with her daughter or somewhere cheaper.
S2.feel: Panicked, like a rig sliding off the bench with no brakes.
S2.quote: There's no other pit in this valley, there's no other job I know how to do, and there's no time.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes every option Carla has: savings, other local jobs, a second household income and the skills for a new role. She doesn't reach for politics, she reaches for welfare and family because that's all that's left. The image of sitting in her daughter's kitchen holding the baby without telling her was quietly devastating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but you can do something with it. The companies and the government should work out a way to get older workers to their pensions. I'd say that if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, which is exactly my plan. So it comes down to whether Kestrel Hill keeps the old rigs running that long. If they put in self-drilling rigs in year two, I'm stuck in the same hole as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor straight out what the plan for the drills is, which I'd normally never do. I'd sell Walter's pickup and put that money away, maybe six thousand. And I'd start doing the Saturday overtime every week while it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. It's better than two years, but I'm betting on someone else's timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd normally never ask the supervisor. What would make you do it this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because not knowing would be worse. I've spent thirty years not asking questions and keeping my head down, and that only works if they still need your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the six thousand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leave it in the bank and not touch it. It's not a plan, it's a cushion, so if they let me go at sixty-one we can limp to the pension. Walter would say put it in a better car, but no.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but you can do something with it. The companies and government should find a way to get older workers to their pensions.
S3.think: Off the record, five years gets me exactly to sixty-three, so it depends on whether Kestrel Hill keeps the old rigs running that long. If self-drilling rigs come in year two, I'm stuck again.
S3.do: Asks her supervisor directly about plans for the drills, which she normally wouldn't do. Sells her husband's pickup to bank about six thousand and works Saturday overtime every week while it lasts.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, because she's betting on someone else's timetable.
S3.quote: I've spent thirty years not asking questions and keeping my head down, and that only works if they still need your head.
S3.fieldNote: Five years technically matches Carla's retirement plan, but she knows the company could automate early and she'd have no backup. She makes the uncharacteristic step of asking her supervisor, which says a lot about the pressure. Her six thousand is a cushion, not a plan, and she is clear about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the young ones to plan, and the old ones should be let go gently. That's fair to everyone. I'm not going to get worked up about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'll be gone by then, sixty-eight and hopefully sitting in the garden with Walter. It's Ines's husband I'd think about, and the grandkids. But for me it's probably fine, if the drill holds out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like I would anyway and save what I can, the twenty a week. I'd tell Ines's husband to look at a trade that needs hands, though I don't know which ones are safe. I wouldn't do any computer courses, there's no point at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly for them, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if the drill holds out'. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with ten years, they might bring the self-drilling rigs in sooner, they were coming anyway. So it's not really the AI that worries me, it's the company getting there first. Ten years for the world isn't ten years for Kestrel Hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Nana drilled holes in a gold mine and was good at feeling the rock. By the time they're grown, they'll think a person drilling a hole by hand is like a person washing clothes in a river.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for the young ones to plan, and the older ones should be let go gently. I wouldn't get worked up about 2036.
S4.think: Privately, I'll be sixty-eight and gone by then, so it's probably fine for me if the drill job holds out. I'd think more about my son-in-law and the grandkids.
S4.do: Carries on working and saves twenty a week. Encourages her son-in-law to look at a hands-on trade, but takes no computer courses herself.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for her family rather than herself.
S4.quote: By the time they're grown, they'll think a person drilling a hole by hand is like a person washing clothes in a river.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Carla's own plan mostly holds, and her worry moves to her daughter's family. She points out that the company could automate drilling before AGI arrives, which is a sharp, practical distinction. She is clear she won't retrain at her age, which fits her resistance to change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt, it'd take everything at once. What would help is a guarantee that if they let older workers go, they pay you through to the pension, so you're not on your knees at the welfare office. I don't need to be rescued, I just need the five years they promised me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the husbands and wives. Walter can't work, so whatever happens to me happens to both of us. People forget it's never just one job in a house.

headlineQuote: I don't need to be rescued, I just need the five years they promised me.
portrait: Carla Fischer is 58 and drills blast holes at the Kestrel Hill gold mine, a careful, repetitive job she likes because it's the same every day. Her husband Walter can't work since his back went, so with about two weeks of savings the household depends on her pay until she retires at sixty-three. She never uses AI tools and struggles even with the site tablet. She's calm when AI is hype, anxious under steady change, panicked when AGI comes in two years and slowly less worried as the warning time grows, though she knows her company could automate drilling early anyway. Pragmatic and modest, she asks for fairness and a bridge to her pension, not a rescue.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take her job, her savings and her husband's security all at once.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that older workers who are let go are paid through to their pension.
